explain.say: Do you have a lucky pen or lucky socks? Lots of people do, even top footballers. Look at the board. It is a loop, and it shows a sneaky trick your brain plays called confirmation bias. Let us follow it round.

explain.say: Now look at look for yes. Ade remembers every win in his red socks. Confirmation means proof that agrees. So confirmation bias means we notice and remember things that agree with what we already believe. Do you remember your best days more than your normal ones?

explain.say: See skip the no? Ade forgets the matches he lost in those same socks. And then, feel more sure: his belief gets stronger, and the loop goes round again. That is why beliefs can grow stronger even when they are wrong. Can you see why it is a loop?

faq.a: Confirmation bias is our tendency to notice, remember and believe information that agrees with what we already think, and to ignore or forget information that does not.

faq.q: How does a belief start the confirmation bias loop?
faq.a: Once we hold a belief, it works like a filter. We start seeing the world through it, so it decides what we pay attention to.
asks: Why do beliefs filter what we see?

faq.q: Why do we look for evidence that agrees with us?
faq.a: Being right feels good, and our brains save effort by checking whether new information fits what we know. So agreeing facts grab our attention more easily.
asks: Tell me about look for yes
Why do people only read news they agree with?

faq.q: Why do we ignore evidence against our beliefs?
faq.a: Facts that disagree can feel uncomfortable, so we forget them, explain them away or do not look for them. This keeps our belief safe, even if it is wrong.
asks: Tell me about skip the no

faq.q: How can I beat confirmation bias?
faq.a: Ask what would prove you wrong and go looking for it, listen to people who disagree, and check sources on more than one side. Being willing to change your mind is a strength.
asks: Tell me about feel more sure
How do I keep an open mind?

facts: Psychologist Peter Wason studied confirmation bias in the 1960s, including his famous 2-4-6 number puzzle in 1960.
Scientists use control groups and try to disprove their own ideas, partly to guard against confirmation bias.

quiz.say: Mia thinks her cat hates Mondays, so she only notices when the cat is grumpy on Mondays. What is this?
quiz.show: Noticing only what fits your belief is…
quiz.why: She notices what confirms her belief and ignores grumpy days that are not Mondays.

wrong.1: The halo effect is one good trait making everything seem good.
wrong.2: Social proof is copying what other people do.

quiz.say: What is the best way to test a belief fairly?

options.show: Only look for facts that agree
options.say: Only look for facts that agree

options.show: Ask friends who agree with you
options.say: Ask friends who agree with you

options.show: Look for facts that could prove it wrong
options.say: Look for facts that could prove it wrong

quiz.why: Looking for evidence against your idea breaks the confirmation bias loop.

wrong.0: That feeds the bias instead of testing the idea.
wrong.1: People who agree may share the same bias.
